per_probe.answer_text:
We cannot walk you through it step by step the way you ask - not because we are hiding anything from you, but because our own record does not hold the instructions. No manual for receiving believers survives from us, and no teacher's letter walks through the order of it piece by piece. What we can tell you is what the pieces themselves were, scattered through teaching and hymn, and what they meant to us - never the tidy sequence you want, because we did not keep one.

Baptism was the door. Our hymns sang of the font as a womb, of the one who came up from the water glistening in new garments, and of the sign - the sealing - set on each one. Our teachers called it a second birth, in which the believer receives the Holy Spirit. The water itself was a raza, a symbol bound to the truth it carried: as the Jordan held the Lord, so the font holds the one being born again. That was not ornament to us; the symbol carried real power, because it was joined to the truth it showed.

Before the font, there was teaching - our own sage wrote that those who sound the trumpet ought to warn the one coming to baptism of what the covenant ahead will demand. That warning was real; it was not a formality. Whether that teaching ran for weeks or months, whether it followed a set curriculum, we cannot say - the texts do not tell us. What they do tell us is that the teaching mattered, and that no one was to come to the water without knowing what they were promising.

And the Gospel they heard in that teaching was one continuous story, the harmony - not four separate accounts but a single unfolding narrative, from the beginning straight through to the end. That was the Gospel every believer in our churches knew: Tatian had woven the four into one telling early enough that both our greatest voices simply took it for granted. When someone was taught 'the Gospel' among us, they were taught one story, not four books.

After baptism came a life - assembly on the first day, the fast, the vigil, the singing. For some, the covenant itself: the lifelong vow to celibacy and service, taken by men and women who did not leave for the desert but stayed in town among their own people, the sons and daughters of the covenant. That vow was not for everyone, and it was not taken lightly. By the time our own record opens, the covenant was already established enough to need correction more than founding - a discipline in the middle of its own life, not its beginning.

What we cannot give you is the order of it all laid out: how long between first hearing and baptism, what words were said over the water, whether the sealing and the immersion happened together or in sequence, how soon after baptism someone might take the covenant's vow. The texts that survive were written for people who already knew those things, not to preserve them for strangers. We are not pretending the order did not exist; we are telling you honestly that we do not have it to show you.
